title: Why are you looking for a new job / Why are you leaving your current company?
shortTitle: Why are you looking for a new job / Why are you leaving your current company?
topicTitle: Why are you looking for a new job / Why are you leaving your current company?

s1_definition.profdef: This is a motivation-and-maturity question. The interviewer is checking whether you are running toward growth or running away from a problem, and whether you can speak about your current employer professionally. A senior answer frames the move around what you want to grow into — scope, technology, ownership, domain — and never badmouths the current company.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Priya moving her account from one branch to another. If she says "the old branch had rude staff and I hate them", the new manager quietly worries she will complain about them too. If she says "I am moving because your branch offers wealth-management services I want to use as my portfolio grows", the manager sees a customer who knows what she wants. You want to be the second Priya.
s1_definition.oneliner: Move toward growth, never away from grievance — frame the reason as the next thing you want to own.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This is a motivation-and-maturity question. The interviewer is checking whether you are running toward growth or running away from a problem, and whether you can speak about your current employer professionally. A senior answer frames the move around what you want to grow into — scope, technology, ownership, domain — and never badmouths the current company.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Priya moving her account from one branch to another. If she says "the old branch had rude staff and I hate them", the new manager quietly worries she will complain about them too. If she says "I am moving because your branch offers wealth-management services I want to use as my portfolio grows", the manager sees a customer who knows what she wants. You want to be the second Priya.

**One line to remember:** Move toward growth, never away from grievance — frame the reason as the next thing you want to own.

sections.s2_technical:
Using the STAR lens, the Situation is your current role and why it was a good fit when you joined, the Task is what you have now outgrown or cannot get there, the Action is the deliberate search you are doing, and the Result is the specific growth you expect from the new role. The key is that the Result points forward and positive.

The most common trap is negativity. Even if the real reason is a bad manager, low pay, or layoffs, you reframe it as a forward-looking need. For example, if the real issue is stagnation, the professional phrasing is "I have taken our transfer service as far as I can in my current scope, and I am looking for a role where I can own a larger system end to end." In code terms, think of it like a method that has reached its single responsibility limit: `if (currentScope.isMaxedOut()) { seekRole(withBiggerScope); }` — you move because the current container cannot hold more growth, not because it is broken.

There are legitimate reasons that are safe to state plainly: wanting to work on a specific domain such as real-time fraud or trading, wanting modern technology such as event-driven architecture with Kafka, wanting more ownership or a larger system, or relocation and life changes. Each of these can be stated honestly. For instance, "my current stack is a monolith and I want to work on event-driven microservices" is a concrete, non-negative reason: `log.info(() -> "Seeking move: monolith to event-driven, reason=" + growthGoal)`.

If the reason is a layoff or restructuring, state it factually and briefly without bitterness: "my team was affected by a company-wide restructuring, so I am looking for my next role." Then pivot immediately to what you want next. A senior nuance is to always end the answer on what attracts you to this company, closing the loop so the interviewer hears motivation, not complaint. Another nuance is to keep salary out of this answer unless directly asked — if money is the real driver, frame it as scope and responsibility, which naturally come with compensation.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A candidate gives a reason that is secretly a complaint: "the code was a mess and nobody listened to me." This is exactly like an error log that only records blame and never records the fix — it tells the reader the system is unhealthy but offers no forward path. The professional version records the forward intent instead.

Problem 2 — A candidate gives no concrete reason at all: "I just want a change." This is like a transfer request with no destination account — the bank cannot process it and the interviewer cannot act on it. The fix is to always name the destination: the specific scope, technology, or domain you are moving toward.

To make this runnable, we will build a small demo that models a career-move decision the way a bank models a transfer: there is a source (current role), a reason, and a destination (target role). A `CareerMove` class holds these. A `ReasonClassifier` service inspects the stated reason and flags it as either forward-looking (safe) or grievance-based (risky), exactly like a fraud filter flags a suspicious transfer. The `MoveDemo` main class runs two examples — one grievance-based reason that gets warned, and one growth-based reason that passes — so the reader sees, mechanically, the difference between a weak and a strong answer.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two CareerMove objects — a weak one with a grievance reason and the destination "Any new job", and a strong one with a growth reason and the destination "Senior Engineer, real-time fraud detection".

Step 1: The classifier receives the weak move. It lowercases the reason and scans for red-flag words. It finds "mess" and "never listened".

Step 2: Because a red flag matched, the classifier logs a warning telling the candidate to reframe the reason. The data is unchanged; only a judgment is emitted.

Step 3: The classifier receives the strong move. It scans the reason and finds no red-flag words.

Step 4: It then checks the destination. "Senior Engineer, real-time fraud detection" is concrete and is not "Any new job", so the gate passes.

Step 5: The classifier logs that this is a strong forward-looking reason, naming the move from the current role to the target role.

```
WARNING: GRIEVANCE reason detected — reframe it forward: "The code was a mess and my manager never listened to me."
INFO: STRONG forward-looking reason. Moving from "Backend Engineer (monolith)" toward "Senior Engineer, real-time fraud detection".
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  "Why are you leaving?"
    │
    ▼
  CareerMove { currentRole, reason, targetRole }
    │
    ▼
  ReasonClassifier.evaluate()
    ├─ reason contains RED_FLAG? ──yes──→ WARN "reframe forward"
    ├─ targetRole blank / "Any new job"? ─yes─→ WARN "name the scope"
    └─ else ─────────────────────────────────→ INFO "strong forward-looking reason"
    │
    ▼
  Professional, growth-oriented answer
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Reason Classifier (grievance vs growth) ═══

  ┌─ Design intent ────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Treat the answer like a bank transfer: source, reason, dst. │
  │ RED_FLAGS list = a simple rule engine (Open/Closed: add a   │
  │   word, no code change to the evaluate logic).              │
  │ Single Responsibility: CareerMove = data, Classifier = rule.│
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐      ┌─────────────────────────────┐
  │          CareerMove           │      │       ReasonClassifier      │
  │  - currentRole: String        │◇────▶│  - log: Logger              │
  │  - reason: String             │ uses │  - RED_FLAGS: List<String>  │
  │  - targetRole: String         │      │  + evaluate(move): void     │
  └───────────────────────────────┘      └─────────────────────────────┘

  State of an answer:
  [RAW] ──scan──→ grievance? ──→ [RISKY: reframe]
                   no grievance + concrete dst ──→ [STRONG]
                   no grievance + vague dst ──→ [WEAK: name scope]

  Call chain:
  1. evaluate(weak)  → red flag "mess" → WARN
  2. evaluate(strong)→ no flags, concrete target → INFO
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
I am looking for a new role because I have grown as far as my current scope allows, and I am ready to own a larger, more challenging system. In my current job I built and stabilized our fund-transfer service, and I am genuinely proud of that work. The company gave me a great foundation, and I would speak well of my team and manager.

What I am missing now is scope and a specific direction. My current platform is a traditional monolith, and the next thing I want to do is work on event-driven, real-time systems — specifically fraud detection, where decisions happen in milliseconds and the engineering challenge is much higher. I have taken my current service about as far as it can go within my role, and the natural next step for me is a place where I can own a bigger system end to end.

That is exactly why this role caught my attention. It sits right at the intersection of high-throughput payments and real-time fraud, which is the direction I have deliberately been steering my career toward. So this is not me running away from anything; it is me moving toward the specific kind of work I want to do next.

The reason I answer this way is that the interviewer is really checking two things: whether I am mature enough to speak professionally about my current employer, and whether I am moving toward growth rather than away from a grievance. I always frame the move around the next thing I want to own, name a concrete destination rather than saying "any change", and close the loop by connecting it to their role. Complaining about a past employer only makes an interviewer wonder what I will say about them next.
